strengths: The paper explores a genuinely novel angle on latent CoT compression: using rendered text images and frozen VLM vision encoders as distillation targets for continuous latent reasoning tokens, distinguishing it from prior latent-CoT works (Coconut, CODI, CoLaR) that learn latent tokens from scratch.
The two-stage training design (frozen alignment stage followed by LoRA latent SFT) is clearly described and the ablations (Table 2, Table 3) show both stages contribute measurably to performance.

Reasonably thorough experimental protocol: multiple backbones (Qwen3-VL-2B/4B, LLaVA-7B), multiple in-domain and OOD datasets, 5 seeds with CIs, and several ablations on rendering configuration, projection head design, and decoding strategy.
The method does deliver substantial token compression (3-4x) and measured wall-clock inference speedups over explicit CoT, which is a well-supported and reproducible empirical claim.
Implementation details (hyperparameters, LoRA config, hardware, seeds) are reported in enough detail to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The paper's central motivating claim — that rendering CoT as images makes latent reasoning 'explicit and traceable' and solves the 'black box' problem — is not actually demonstrated. At inference, the model never produces or decodes an actual image or human-readable text; the 'visualizations' offered as evidence of interpretability (Figs. 6-9) are generic embedding statistics (heatmaps, cosine-similarity matrices, norm/mean/std plots) that are not qualitatively different from what could be produced for any latent vector, visual or not, and provide no verified mapping back to the original reasoning content. No experiment shows a human or automatic decoder recovering meaningful rendered text/logic from the latent embeddings to substantiate 'traceability.'

The core mechanistic hypothesis — that specifically *visual* rendering of text (as opposed to any other frozen high-capacity encoder's representation of the same text, e.g., a frozen text encoder) is what drives the benefit — is untested. No ablation isolates the vision-specific contribution from the general benefit of an additional pretrained-encoder distillation signal, leaving open the possibility that any suitably rich auxiliary target would produce similar gains, which would undercut the paper's 'visual latent reasoning' framing.

RoT consistently and substantially underperforms explicit CoT in absolute accuracy (e.g., 55.4% vs 79.3% average on Qwen3-VL-4B; 33.2% vs 55.8% on MATH), which is a large gap inconsistent with the abstract's characterization of 'competitive performance.'

The comparison against LLM-based latent-reasoning baselines (Table 2) is potentially confounded: RoT uses a VLM backbone with an additional vision encoder and projection head (more capacity/parameters) versus plain LLM baselines that have no access to any visual component at all, so the superior OOD robustness attributed to 'visual semantic supervision' could partly reflect this capacity/architecture asymmetry rather than the claimed mechanism. Additionally, the CODI baseline's reported accuracy (e.g., 7-18%) is dramatically lower than in its original paper, raising concern about baseline reproduction fidelity.

Dynamic termination via the learned special token performs very poorly (single-digit accuracy, Table 4) versus fixed token budgets, indicating the proposed method lacks a practical, task-agnostic stopping criterion; the fixed-budget workaround itself requires per-dataset tuning (32 vs. 64 tokens), which is an unresolved practicality gap that limits real-world deployability.

The paper's contribution claims ('first framework to reify reasoning chain... making latent reasoning explicit and traceable') appear overstated relative to what is empirically shown, given the above concerns about unverified interpretability and the accuracy trade-off.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the two-stage training pipeline (visual alignment then latent SFT) is described in enough detail to be largely reproducible, with LoRA/optimizer hyperparameters, rendering configuration, and dataset splits given in the appendix.

A reasonably thorough set of ablations is provided (projection-head activation/dimension, rendering height/font/padding, decoding strategy, stage-wise ablation), which helps isolate the contribution of individual design choices.

The idea of using a frozen pretrained vision encoder as a fixed semantic target for latent CoT compression is a modestly interesting engineering choice that avoids training visual tokens from scratch and is tested across three VLM backbones (Qwen3-VL-2B/4B, LLaVA-7B) and five datasets, showing some generality of the pipeline.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim of the paper — that rendering CoT as images makes latent reasoning "explicit and traceable" and solves the analyzability problem of prior implicit-CoT methods — is never actually demonstrated. At inference time the model only emits latent vision-like embeddings; these are never decoded back into a human-readable image or text, and the "analysis" offered in Sec. 4.4/Appendix D consists solely of heatmaps, cosine-similarity matrices, and summary statistics of the latent vectors, which are exactly the same post-hoc diagnostics one could compute for any opaque latent-CoT method (Coconut, CODI, etc.). The paper does not show that a human can recover or verify the reasoning content from these visualizations, so the core selling point relative to prior implicit CoT work is unsubstantiated.

The abstract and results text repeatedly describe RoT as achieving "competitive performance" against explicit CoT, but the reported numbers show large accuracy drops (e.g., Qwen3-VL-4B: 79.3% vs 55.4% average Pass@1 on grade-school tasks, a 24-point gap; 55.8% vs 33.2% on MATH, a 22-point gap). Characterizing this as "competitive" is an overstatement of the evidence and should be reframed as an efficiency/accuracy trade-off rather than a maintained-performance claim.

The method's own proposed dynamic termination mechanism (via the <|img_end|> special token), which is architecturally central to the framework, essentially fails in practice (3.87% vs 37.8% for the best fixed budget on GSM8k-Aug), forcing the authors to fall back on manually tuned, dataset-specific fixed token budgets. This undermines the "plug-and-play" and general-purpose framing, since practitioners must grid-search an optimal budget per dataset/task without a principled way to select it.

The LLM-based latent-reasoning baselines used for comparison (iCoT, Coconut, CODI) score implausibly low (e.g., CODI 9.7% and iCoT 25.9% average accuracy on grade-school tasks) relative to their reported results in the original papers, raising concerns about whether these baselines were faithfully reproduced or tuned; this makes the claimed 8.1% improvement over the "best" baseline (CoLaR-2) less convincing given the apparent weakness of the other reproduced baselines.

In several settings the improvement over a trivial "SFT without any CoT" baseline is marginal (e.g., LLaVA: 11.2% vs 12.4%; GSM-Hard on Qwen3-VL-4B: 9.48% vs 14.1%), which questions how much of the latent visual channel is contributing real reasoning versus incidental capacity/regularization effects.

No statistical significance testing accompanies the reported confidence intervals, and cross-architecture results (LLaVA-7B) show substantially degraded absolute performance and smaller relative gains, suggesting limited robustness of the approach across different vision encoders/backbones.

The formalization in Sec. 3.3.1 is imprecise (the index t is overloaded to denote both an autoregressive reasoning step and an index into the K vision-embedding targets), obscuring exactly how variable-length latent generation is aligned against a fixed-length rendered-image embedding sequence.

The work is not compared against any of the closely related "text-as-image" context-compression methods discussed in Related Work (e.g., Glyph, PixelWorld), despite the paper's core mechanism (rendering text to images and encoding via a vision encoder) being conceptually very close to that line of work; such a comparison (or clear differentiation with numbers) is needed to support the novelty claims.

strengths: The paper proposes a reasonably novel idea: rendering CoT text into images and using a frozen pre-trained VLM vision encoder as a distillation target for a lightweight projection head, avoiding costly new pre-training and enabling a 'plug-and-play' upgrade path for existing VLMs.

Experiments span three different VLM backbones (Qwen3-VL-2B/4B, LLaVa-1.6-7B) and five datasets (in-domain GSM8k-Aug plus OOD GSM-Hard/SVAMP/MultiArith/MATH), with results reported over five seeds with 95% CIs, which is good statistical practice for this subfield.

Reasonably thorough ablations are provided: two-stage training necessity, rendering configuration (image height/font/padding, single-line vs square layout), projection-head activation/hidden-dim choices, and decoding strategy (fixed budget vs dynamic termination), which help isolate design choices.

Token compression and inference-time speedups are clearly quantified and are non-trivial (e.g., 8.55s→1.84s on GSM-Hard), which is a concrete practical benefit if the accuracy trade-off is acceptable for a given application.
The paper is generally clearly written with a coherent narrative and includes a candid limitations section covering language/domain scope, manual token-budget tuning, and training overhead.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim of 'analyzability via visualization'/'making the latent rationale explicit and traceable' is never actually demonstrated: at inference no image is rendered or decoded from the latent embeddings, and the qualitative analysis in Sec. 4.4/Appendix D only inspects abstract embedding statistics (heatmaps, cosine-similarity matrices, norms) rather than showing that the latent trajectory can be decoded back into human-readable reasoning content. This undercuts the paper's main selling point relative to prior opaque latent-CoT methods.

The abstract/intro claim of 'maintaining competitive performance' against explicit CoT is not well supported by the actual numbers: on harder tasks the accuracy gap is very large (e.g., GSM-Hard 14.1% vs 53.4%, MATH 33.2% vs 55.8%, GSM8k-Aug roughly half of SFT-CoT), which is a substantial degradation, not near-parity performance; only on the easiest dataset (MultiArith) is the gap small. The framing in the abstract/conclusion appears to overstate the strength of the empirical results.

The comparison against LLM-based latent-reasoning baselines (Table 2) uses a text-only Qwen3-4B-Instruct backbone for baselines versus a Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct backbone for RoT; since the VLM backbone brings additional vision-related parameters/pretraining, the reported advantage over CoLaR/Coconut/CODI is confounded and cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed rendering/alignment mechanism rather than to using a different (possibly stronger) base model.

The dynamic termination strategy (the more 'natural' inference mode using the learned end-of-thought token) fails dramatically (e.g., 3.87% vs the fixed-budget optimum of 37.8% on GSM8k-Aug), and the fixed-budget alternative requires manual, dataset-specific tuning of the latent length, weakening the practicality and 'plug-and-play' framing of the method.

Evaluation is restricted to English-language grade-school/competition math and simple logical benchmarks; no results are given for commonsense/other reasoning domains, and no comparison of the added training-time cost (rendering + vision encoding + two-stage training) is quantified against baselines, leaving the overall cost-benefit picture incomplete.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely efficiency problem (verbose CoT reasoning) and proposes a reasonably novel mechanism: using a frozen VLM vision encoder as a regression target to structure a compressed latent reasoning space, avoiding training reasoning tokens from scratch.

Experiments span three VLM backbones (Qwen3-VL-2B/4B, LLaVa-Mistral-7B) and multiple datasets (GSM8k-Aug, GSM-Hard, SVAMP, MultiArith, MATH, plus GPQA/ProsQA in the appendix), providing reasonably broad empirical coverage.

Extensive ablations are provided (projection head activation/dimension, rendering configuration such as font size/height/padding, decoding strategy, two-stage training necessity), which supports some of the design choices and aids reproducibility.
Reported results include confidence intervals over 5 seeds, training-cost comparisons, and inference-time measurements, which is good experimental practice.
The comparison against LLM-based latent reasoning baselines (Coconut, CODI, CoLaR) on a matched VLM backbone (Appendix E) is a useful control to isolate the source of gains.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim — that rendering CoT as images makes latent reasoning 'explicit, traceable, and analyzable,' addressing the 'black box' problem — is not actually substantiated. At inference, no images are generated or decoded; the model only produces continuous hidden states aligned (via a frozen projection head) to a vision-embedding space. The paper's own analysis in Sec. 4.4 relies on abstract statistics (heatmaps, cosine-similarity matrices, embedding norms) rather than any human-readable reconstruction of the latent content, so the interpretability claim in the title/abstract is not delivered by the evidence shown.

The efficiency-accuracy trade-off is much weaker than the framing suggests: e.g., on Qwen3-VL-4B, RoT achieves 55.4% average accuracy vs. 79.3% for explicit CoT (a ~24-point drop) for 3.4x token compression, and on MATH, 33.2% vs. 55.8% (a ~23-point drop). Describing this as 'competitive accuracy' and a 'Pareto exploration' overstates what is actually a substantial accuracy sacrifice, particularly on harder tasks (MATH, GSM-Hard) where the compressed model barely beats the no-CoT baseline.

Some reproduced baseline numbers look anomalous and undermine confidence in the comparisons: CODI achieves only 7-9% on GSM8k-Aug/MultiArith with Qwen3-4B-Instruct, well below even the no-CoT baseline and far below the numbers typically reported for CODI in prior literature, suggesting a possible implementation or hyperparameter issue in the reproduction rather than a genuine capability gap.

No ablation isolates whether the specific choice of 'vision-encoder embeddings as target' is necessary, versus simply using any fixed, pre-trained high-dimensional embedding space (e.g., frozen text embeddings, or embeddings from an unrelated network) as a regularization anchor. Without this control, it is unclear whether the reported gains stem from the visual modality specifically or merely from having *some* informative, frozen external anchor to structure the latent space — a claim central to the paper's framing.

The method is not compared empirically against the token-selection/RL-based CoT compression methods discussed at length in Related Work (TokenSkip, LightThinker, R1-Compress, C3oT, VeriThinker), so the practical competitiveness of visual latent compression versus these more established and likely stronger baselines remains unassessed.

Dynamic termination (the more practically desirable, adaptive stopping mechanism) is shown to fail badly (e.g., 3.87% vs. 37.8% Pass@1 on GSM8k-Aug), and the paper falls back on manually-tuned fixed token budgets that differ per dataset (32 vs. 64), which weakens the claimed 'plug-and-play' and general applicability of the approach and is acknowledged only as a limitation to be addressed 'in future work.'

The 'plug-and-play, no additional pre-training' claim is somewhat overstated given that the method still requires substantial two-stage fine-tuning on large task-specific data (e.g., 385k training samples for GSM8k-Aug) plus online rendering and vision-encoder forward passes, incurring ~1.5x the training cost of standard SFT-CoT.
The code availability link/footnote appears broken or missing ('Our code is available a'), raising minor reproducibility concerns despite otherwise detailed hyperparameter reporting.

strengths: The paper tackles a real efficiency problem (verbose CoT) and proposes a conceptually interesting idea of using rendered-text visual embeddings as a supervision/anchor signal for latent reasoning, which is a reasonably novel combination of 'text-as-image' and 'latent CoT' lines of work.

Experimental coverage is broad: three VLM backbones (Qwen3-VL-2B/4B, LLaVA-1.6-7B), five math datasets plus GPQA/ProsQA, multiple LLM- and VLM-based latent reasoning baselines, and results reported with 5 seeds and 95% CIs, which supports reproducibility.

Reasonably thorough ablations (projection head activation/dimension, rendering font size/height/padding, decoding strategy, two-stage training components, training cost, unified-backbone comparison) that help isolate some design choices.
Appendix provides substantial implementation detail (LoRA config, optimizer, special-token initialization, hardware) which aids reproducibility.
Honest reporting of failure cases and the dynamic-termination instability, and transparent discussion of limitations.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim – that RoT makes the latent rationale 'explicit and traceable' and solves the 'black box' problem – is not actually substantiated: at inference time no images are rendered or decoded; the model still produces continuous latent vectors whose only connection to interpretability is a training-time regression target. No experiment decodes/inverts latents back to readable text or images, nor is there any human or quantitative evaluation of interpretability, so this key selling point is asserted but not demonstrated.

The claimed 'competitive efficiency-accuracy Pareto' is overstated given the data: on Qwen3-VL-4B, accuracy drops from 79.3% (explicit CoT) to 55.4% (RoT), a ~24-point loss, and on MATH from 55.8% to 33.2% (loss of over 20 points); for LLaVA-7B, RoT (12.4%) is barely above the no-CoT baseline (11.2%) despite the added architecture and training complexity, suggesting the method provides little real reasoning benefit on that backbone.

A crucial ablation is missing: there is no baseline that distills/aligns the latent reasoning states to compressed *textual* embeddings (rather than rendered-image embeddings) with the same training recipe. Without this, it is not established that the 'visual' aspect itself (rather than simply the existence of an external dense supervisory target distilled via a frozen encoder) is responsible for the reported gains over Coconut/CODI/CoLaR.

The 'Pass@1/#L' efficiency metric used to declare superiority is non-standard and somewhat arbitrary (a ratio that can favor near-zero-token/low-accuracy regimes); more standard accuracy-vs-compute trade-off curves or fixed-accuracy-budget comparisons would be more convincing evidence.

Method is reported to be quite sensitive to rendering hyperparameters (font size, image height, padding) and requires per-dataset tuning of the latent token budget (32 vs 64), which raises concerns about robustness/generalizability and practical deployability as claimed ('plug-and-play').

Training cost is actually ~1.5x higher than SFT-CoT (56.1h vs 36.9h in Table 7), which is in some tension with the abstract's framing of avoiding 'additional overhead,' even though the paper does clarify this refers to pretraining rather than fine-tuning.

OOD generalization claims rest on a narrow set of simple arithmetic variants (GSM-Hard, SVAMP, MultiArith) and two additional small-scale datasets (GPQA, ProsQA) with near-ceiling or saturated results (e.g., ProsQA at 100%), limiting the strength of generalization claims to 'logical reasoning' more broadly.

Some presentation issues: Figure 1 and parts of Section 3 are dense and the two-stage pipeline notation (e.g., reuse of index t in Eq. 1) is occasionally unclear, and the paper does not report standard baselines' statistical variance in Table 2/3 in a way that is easy to compare against RoT's reported CIs.

strengths: The core idea—using a frozen VLM vision encoder as a supervision target to structure a continuous latent-reasoning space—is a reasonably novel angle within the implicit CoT literature, avoiding the need to learn a latent codebook from scratch.

Extensive experimentation: three different base models (Qwen3-VL-2B/4B, LLaVa-1.6-7B), multiple in-domain and OOD math datasets, an additional MATH benchmark, a unified-backbone comparison against Coconut/CODI/CoLaR to control for VLM pretraining effects, and extension to non-math tasks (GPQA, ProsQA).

Thorough ablations on architecture and rendering hyperparameters (projection head activation/width, image height/font/padding, decoding strategy, fixed vs dynamic termination, two-stage training necessity), which support the specific design choices made.
Reports confidence intervals over multiple runs and includes wall-clock inference-time comparisons, adding some rigor to the efficiency claims.
Honest limitations section acknowledging the instability of dynamic termination, the need for task-specific token-budget tuning, and added training overhead.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'analyzability via visualization' / making the rationale 'explicit and traceable' is not actually substantiated: at inference the model never produces or decodes an interpretable image or text from the latent tokens—only heatmaps/statistics of the continuous embeddings are shown post hoc. This is a central contribution of the abstract/intro that the experiments do not directly support.

The reported accuracy gap relative to explicit CoT is large in several settings (e.g., MATH: 33.2% vs 55.8% on Qwen3-VL-4B; average GSM-family: 55.4% vs 79.3%), which is difficult to reconcile with the paper's framing of 'competitive accuracy' and a favorable 'efficiency-accuracy Pareto'—the trade-off is real but arguably oversold in the writing.

A key ablation is missing: whether the improvement stems specifically from the visual/rendering pathway versus simply having any frozen, structured external embedding space as an alignment target (e.g., a frozen text encoder or even a fixed random but structured target). Without this control, the causal attribution to 'vision embeddings as semantic anchors' is not fully isolated.

Dynamic termination via the special token fails dramatically (e.g., 3.87% vs 37.8% Pass@1 on GSM8k-Aug), and the manuscript both frames this as a general property of continuous latent spaces (citing LVR) and relies exclusively on a manually tuned fixed-budget alternative; this undermines the practicality/plug-and-play claim and is a nontrivial robustness gap not fully resolved.

In-domain performance is sometimes not better than existing latent-reasoning baselines (e.g., CoLaR-2 outperforms RoT on GSM8k-Aug, 40.0 vs 37.8), with RoT's advantage concentrated in OOD generalization and average scores; the narrative sometimes reads as though RoT is uniformly superior.

Training cost, added architectural complexity (requiring a full VLM with vision encoder rather than pure LLM), and the need for per-dataset token-budget calibration somewhat offset the plug-and-play efficiency narrative, though these are honestly disclosed in the limitations.
